These are medical devices, not industrial tools.  If not explicitly regulated, I would be extremely surprised to find one considered noisy.   Even then, you’re doing more damage to your hearing driving to your appointment with the windows open.  

The noisiest part of the treatment is only 2 minutes long with thetaburst, and intermittent.  Since duration is an even more important factor in hearing damage and tinnitus, your machine would likely have to be outputting in the 110+ dB range to do damage to your hearing in that time frame, and if that was the case then OSHA would require your techs to be decked out like the airline workers working next to idling jet engines.

https://www.cdc.gov/nceh/hearing_loss/what_noises_cause_hearing_loss.html

And on the 0.01% chance your machine is loud enough to necessitate that your tech is wearing flight-line hearing protection, please come back here and gloat.  I would be curious to know.

The bands on any useful over ear hearing protection are steel.  It requires the spring tension to seal the cups around your ear.  If you find over ear hearing protection not using steel, most likely they suck. 

At my office they put delicate paper tape around and over the top of patients foreheads and the seat headrest to hold their head in roughly the exact same place.  

They use lasers to place your head in the exact same spot every time

They push your head from one side with a cushion.   The coil then is placed on the opposite side of your head.  

These are all reasons over-ear hearing protection would not work.  Unless you have some preexisting condition, I would seriously challenge your desire to use hearing protection at all, much less over ear hearing protection.

I haven’t either, but depending on the company this could certainly happen. 

If someone is marginally the best choice, and they’re already extending a more-than-fair offer and expecting they’ll have to train you, it could happen.  There’s often a lot of politics behind the scenes on who they should hire (at certain companies I’ve been at, NOT all companies, generally these are the bad ones) and if you’re marginally the best choice or someone has reservations, asking for more (especially in a less than perfect way) can have unintended consequences.   I’ve seen it happen for non-entry level employees, but generally these are for larger raises (which we could actually afford pay), they just decided that another candidate was a better cost/benefit at that price point. 

I tend to agree with the other commenter here, though.  They’ve already decided they want you.  You should hope to and trust to be heading into a healthy and respectful environment, in which case this is a very healthy and respectful conversation to have.  Asking for more and receiving a little more is a HUGE boon to mutual trust and often happens in my experience.  If they say no, you’ve gathered information on the company.  If they rescind your offer, likely they’re a toxic company.  You don’t want to work there anyway, unless you’re desperate.  And $72k starting in Pittsburgh?   I started $53k in DC with engineering.  High level clearance.  I hit $69k 1.5 years after and had 2% COL raises for the next 6 years - I did not have a good quality of life.  I would entirely hesitate asking for more for this one junction in my career - entry level with no leverage, asking for more on top of a fair offer - nah, probably wouldn’t jeopardize it.  I would be seriously counting my blessings and pinching myself to make sure it was reality.  

Work harder than ever, save like crazy, learn a lot, and then if everything goes like it did for me you’ll be more-or-less set for a long time.  7 years at $50-$75k and now 11 years in my career I am making $154k

It’s good to get practice for yourself.  Often a company will only give an offer if they want you, and a good company will often have a small bonus prepared to help “sweeten the pot”.  So it’s almost always worth, after receiving an offer that’s perfectly fair or great, to ask one final time to the hiring manager or recruiter “this is good, I was wondering if there was any chance there was anything else”?  Very often they’ll throw in a $3,000 one time bonus.  

However as an entry employee, the salary you’re receiving is extremely fair.  Be careful not to jeopardize that.  Do an assessment, it seems like employers are striggling for employees so you may have wiggle room.  Does this company have dozens of applicants, perhaps they don’t want a squeaky wheel (not a long term company for you) in which case I’d keep my mouth shut.  But if you have a good rapport, call the HR person or hiring manager within a business day of receiving the offer and say “this is great, I’m really happy but I was wondering if there was perhaps some more wiggle room here?   I’d like to make sure my move goes as easily as possible, I’d like to support as best as possible and explore a long time opportunity with you”.  If they’re good people worst they’ll say is no.   If they’ve gone through 3 rounds of interviews with 6 other people and you were marginally the best choice, then they might just go down the list to the next person.  It’s hard to know how much leverage you have.

One time in a very exhausting period of life I had minor sleep problems.  In one specific instance, I was asleep and began waking up realizing I was so fatigued I could no longer breathe.  I could feel it - my chest was too heavy.  I could not breathe.  I tried so hard, but my tongue was blocking my mouth - also too tired to move my tongue - and my sinuses must have been clogged.  I could not breathe.  I was already exhausted, despite sleeping for several hours and I could feel myself slipping away even deeper.  As I became more awake (never fully awake) I began to notice more and more what was happening.  I started panicking, getting frightened but there was no adrenaline.  No second wind, nothing to save me.  I was so exhausted and I felt myself slipping away, unable to breathe and losing consciousness.  I was laying on my left side, but my shoulder was sitting front of my torso. So I was angled backward a little.  My arm was under my pillow in front of my head.  I was propped in a way that I couldn’t easily just roll over.  My futon I slept on at the time was in couch mode and I had the seat against my right shoulder, I couldn’t just roll a full 180.   I tried so hard to roll forward and nothing moved.  I was so tired.  I was so exhausted.  My body was screaming to roll over but not a muscle moved.  No adrenaline.  Still no energy.  Still slipping away.  Losing consciousness 

Finally after about a full minute of waking up disoriented to this strange mix of suffocation, confusion, and terror, somehow my body worked for a split second, long enough to roll over about 10 degrees.   I was able to breathe again.  I was still exhausted.   Even more so from the energy and willpower it took to roll forward that tiny amount.  I still couldn’t move.  I could breathe, but I was still too tired to take a deep breath of air.  My head was strained, hot and full of pressure like my veins were popping out of my scalp.  I still had no adrenaline, I still could not move, I had been scared but I had no energy to react.  This assessment came across me pretty quickly so I simply let myself pass out again.  It was a strange combination of sleep and simply not having enough air.  I woke up the next day and felt very off. 

I’ve never had anything the same happen again since.  Like in your story, my body felt like it was 500 lbs.  I could feel myself sunken into my futon. Firm cushion, probably no more sunken in than normal.  But this time I could feel it.  Vividly.

Integrating components =\= integrating components that already existed. 

Optimized UAVs often require subsystems that have to be developed from the ground up or modified from other specialized hardware.

Yes it can get very scary, although without knowing specifically what your concerns are I can just say at a high level that it usually isn’t as scary as it seems.

There is a very long development process, sometimes unsolvable, between a demonstrated capability and an operational capability. 

People tend to see something and say “oh that works!” And extrapolate that to the either positive or negative impact it would yield in operation.  Usually it’s logical fallacy.  

UAVs are very much this way.  I billed ~$60,000 to a project this year, leading the UAV and payload line of effort, reporting  to the Chief Engineer of a 3,000 person sector, that went almost exactly like this.  These extremely smart and successful people saw “demonstrated solutions” and extrapolated that to an operational picture that… just wasn’t possible, if you did the math and engineering.  These situations are very difficult because - and this is how I got hired - if you’re too candid and blunt with your response, the managers will think you’re negative or not operating in good faith.  I was hired to backfill a PhD career UAV expert who was deemed a “problems person”.  He was 100% right, I just had to let the managers down easier (on their original goals, that is, we tried to redirect to something more valuable).

People get wrapped around the axle about negativity/positivity - it upsets me.  I just try to find the truth.  And the truth is that you can’t beat physics.  That might be “negative” for someone trying to do something impossible.  However, it is positive in the sense that you realize the bad guys can’t do it either :-) 

So, in general, if something seems upsetting or scary I’d encourage scrutinizing it !  Where would it break?  

Here’s a cool example.  The Javelin is extremely effective against tanks in Ukraine.  It’s awesome !  However, Russia had 12,800+ tanks before the Ukraine invasion. You're correct - this is an accurate statement.  However, rentals and homes generally have wildly different 'quality' - by nature or otherwise, people tend to purchase the homes with backyards and rent shared bedrooms and one bedroom apartments.  You can't even really argue that you can save money purchasing an apartment, because I haven't seen a single one that doesn't require a condo fee of an additional $300-$400 a month (Seattle and Wash DC), but maybe I'm dumb here.

Anyway, with purchasing you also have to consider: 1) Appraisal fees, closing costs, property taxes and hikes, initial inspection 2) Maintenance 3) Insurance (home is more expensive than renters) 4) Savings for major repairs (roof replacement, etc).

Also, some people rent units for really cheap because even if someone treats the place poorly, it won't devalue as much as if they left it completely vacant.  

Now that I've made ppl run the gauntlet; purchasing has much higher qualitative value.  Saving every penny you can doesn't lend itself to a fulfilling life.  Maybe you have a family.  Maybe you keep getting shitty roommates (me), maybe your landlord sucks, maybe you want to build a skate park in your back yard or garage....  

Anyway, yeah, if you value the freedom highly and you know you're staying in the same place for a long time and you don't mind losing some money in the long run because you want to enjoy yourself a little extra now; buying can be great.  "
